# From Research to Practice

<!-- This file is the source of a page on the course website. Read it there: https://ai.buas.nl/open-courses/introduction-to-ml/self-study/theme-6/03_from_research_to_practice.html -->

**Estimated time: approximately 6 hours**

Machine learning research is most useful when you can translate ideas from the literature into concrete decisions in your own work.

In this activity, you will read an accessible machine learning paper, identify useful principles, and apply at least one of them to a machine learning project of your own.

After completing the activity, you should be able to:

- read a machine learning research paper more effectively;
- identify ideas that are relevant to an applied problem;
- translate a research principle into a concrete modeling decision;
- evaluate whether the change actually improves your approach.

## Read — approximately 1 hour

Read:

[A Few Useful Things to Know About Machine Learning](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~pedrod/papers/cacm12.pdf) (Domingos, *Communications of the ACM*, 2012; [journal version](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2347736.2347755))

Take notes as you read.

Rather than trying to remember every detail, identify principles that could influence how you develop or evaluate a machine learning system.

## Apply

Choose **at least one principle from the paper** and apply it to a machine learning project of your own: a project you are working on, or one of the models you built in the Self-study notebooks.

Document:

1. which principle you selected;
2. why it is relevant to your project;
3. what you changed;
4. how you evaluated the effect: compare the model with and without the change under the same validation, on the same cross-validation folds, and keep the test set for the final check;
5. what you learned from the result.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## An example of such a write-up (with made-up numbers)
1. Principle: "More data beats a cleverer algorithm."
2. Relevance: my classifier was trained on 300 samples from one source, and I had a second source with 200 more samples that I had not used.
3. Change: I added the second source to the training data and kept the model and its settings the same.
4. Evaluation: 5-fold cross-validation on the same folds of the data I want to predict, before and after: macro-F1 0.71 ± 0.04 before, 0.78 ± 0.05 after.
5. What I learned: the gain is larger than the spread over the folds, so it is probably real. A more complex model on the old data had given only 0.72.
:::

If your project contains several trained models, **ensembling** is one useful idea to explore.

You could combine predictions from multiple models, compare the ensemble against your best individual model, and investigate whether—and why—the result changes.

The goal is not to prove that the paper's recommendation always works.

The goal is to move from:

**“I read an interesting idea.”**

to:

**“I tested the idea in my own context and collected evidence about whether it helped.”**
